hook.text: Andrew Carnegie built 2,509 libraries worldwide. He also crushed unions and paid steelworkers starvation wages.

buildup.text: Philanthropy has always served dual purposes: genuine altruism and strategic reputation laundering.

discovery.text: The 'Giving Pledge' asks billionaires to donate half their wealth. Over 200 have signed—but few have delivered.

twist.text: Effective altruism argues most philanthropy is wasteful. A malaria net saves more lives per dollar than an opera house.

climax.text: Tax deductions turn charity into a profitable activity. The giver saves money while choosing where public funds go.

punchline.text: Generosity and self-interest share more DNA than we admit.

quiz.question: How many libraries did Andrew Carnegie build?

details.summary: Large-scale philanthropy functions as gift-giving at the highest level of social status — naming rights on buildings, charitable galas, and public donation pledges all convert wealth into social prestige. From Andrew Carnegie to the Giving Pledge, philanthropic gifts are never purely altruistic.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding philanthropy as status-driven gift-giving reveals that the world's largest charitable acts are simultaneously acts of social positioning. Pure altruism and strategic self-interest are inseparable.
takeaways: Andrew Carnegie gave away 90% of his fortune to build his legacy
The Giving Pledge asks billionaires to donate the majority of wealth
Naming rights convert donations into permanent public recognition

faq.question: Is big philanthropy truly generous?
faq.answer: Critics like Anand Giridharadas argue that billionaire philanthropy allows the wealthy to shape society according to their preferences while receiving tax benefits and public adoration. The same systems that create extreme wealth often create the problems philanthropy claims to solve.

faq.question: What is the Giving Pledge?
faq.answer: Launched by Warren Buffett and Bill and Melinda Gates in 2010, the Giving Pledge asks billionaires to commit to giving away the majority of their wealth during their lifetime or in their will. Over 200 billionaires have signed. It is not legally binding — it is a public moral commitment.
